meta.subtitle: A 30 / 60 / 90-day path to standardise shop-floor execution across APAC

slides.title: One RetailCo, 120 Stores
slides.subtitle: A 30 / 60 / 90-day path to standardise shop-floor execution across APAC
slides.script: We are starting from a simple operating premise: RetailCo should feel like one business to customers, staff, and leaders, even across 120 APAC stores. Today, the pain points tell us that each branch is improvising its own version of visibility, selling, onboarding, and rostering coordination. Our proposal is not to add another dashboard for its own sake. We want to create a standard operating loop: see what happens, hear what is said, codify what works, and roll that into repeatable action.

slides.text: RetailCo is not running 120 stores; it is running 120 versions of the store.
slides.script: We think this is the sentence worth remembering. When the COO says, "I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor," that is not only a reporting problem. It is a standardisation problem. When the best managers outsell the worst ones by 3x, that is not only a talent problem. It is a replication problem. The work is to stop excellence being local, personal, and accidental, and make it visible enough that every store can run closer to the same RetailCo standard.

slides.title: The consistency gap is already measurable

metrics.label: frontline staff depending on local routines
sales gap between best and worst managers

slides.script: We do not need to invent a burning platform here; RetailCo has already named it. One hundred and twenty stores create reach, but they also create 120 chances for different habits to take hold. Two thousand frontline staff need the same answers, coaching, and onboarding patterns, not whatever happens to be available on shift. And the 3x manager gap tells us there is know-how inside the business already. The question is how we expose it, score it, and turn it into the way RetailCo works everywhere.

slides.title: Each pain maps to a standardisation lever

cards.heading: Floor visibility
cards.body: Spacesight shows real activity same day, not Monday spreadsheets.

cards.heading: Customer conversations
cards.body: Echo captures and scores what staff actually say.

cards.heading: Manager know-how
cards.body: Harbor Wiki turns best practice into reusable playbooks.

cards.heading: Rostering friction
cards.body: Discovery scopes workflow; no core scheduling product today.

slides.script: We want to be precise about product fit. Spacesight directly addresses the COO’s Monday spreadsheet problem by showing what is happening on the floor through in-store vision analytics. Echo answers the missing conversation layer by capturing and scoring how frontline staff talk to customers. Harbor Wiki, the AI Wiki, bottles the moves of the best managers so new hires and weaker stores can look them up. Scheduling is different. We do not have a roster engine in this stack, so we will treat it honestly as a discovery workstream around workflow, handoffs, and integration options.

slides.title: 30 days: replace lag with visibility

rows.right: Leading signals appear during the week
Coordination steps mapped with operations team

slides.script: The first 30 days are about removing the blindfold. We are not promising RetailCo a finished transformation in month one. We are promising that the COO should not have to wait until Monday to learn what happened last week. Spacesight gives us a floor activity signal, and Echo gives us the customer conversation signal. Together, they let us compare stores on observable behaviours, not only end results. At the same time, we map the rostering coordination path so we understand where the pain is process, ownership, or tooling.

slides.title: 30-day instrumentation plan

cards.heading: Spacesight baseline
cards.body: Identify floor events worth standardising across stores.

cards.heading: Echo baseline
cards.body: Capture the selling language customers actually hear.

cards.heading: Store comparison
cards.body: Compare best and weaker stores on observable actions.

cards.heading: Rostering map
cards.body: Trace approvals, inputs, changes, and handoffs.

slides.script: We would use the first horizon to agree what a good store looks like in data. With Spacesight, we identify the floor events that matter to RetailCo’s operating model. With Echo, we capture the language and service behaviours that separate strong selling from weak execution. Then we compare high and low performing stores on what people actually do, not on generic best-practice theory. For scheduling, we capture the real coordination map: who supplies inputs, who approves, where changes happen, and where teams lose time.

slides.title: 60 days: turn evidence into one operating standard

cards.heading: See
cards.body: Spacesight defines the recurring floor patterns worth managing.

cards.heading: Hear
cards.body: Echo identifies conversation behaviours that should be coached.

cards.heading: Codify
cards.body: Harbor Wiki converts the best routines into searchable guidance.

slides.script: By day 60, the aim shifts from observation to standard setting. We take what Spacesight shows about the floor and what Echo reveals about customer conversations, then separate signal from noise. The point is not to punish stores for being different; it is to decide which differences matter. Harbor Wiki becomes the place where the business bottles the best manager behaviours: opening routines, customer approaches, escalation patterns, and coaching prompts. That starts turning RetailCo’s strongest local habits into a shared operating memory.

slides.title: 60-day routines that make standards stick

cards.heading: Manager coaching
cards.body: Use Echo scores to coach specific selling behaviours.

cards.heading: Floor huddles
cards.body: Use Spacesight patterns to focus daily priorities.

cards.heading: New-hire answers
cards.body: Use Harbor Wiki instead of whoever is rostered.

cards.heading: Roster workflow
cards.body: Validate scheduling ownership and escalation points.

slides.script: Standards only matter if they enter the rhythm of the store. At 60 days, we would make the insights practical for managers and frontline teams. Echo can guide coaching on the exact selling behaviours that show up in conversations. Spacesight can focus daily huddles on what is happening on the floor, not what someone remembers. Harbor Wiki reduces dependence on whichever colleague happens to be working that day. On rostering, we keep the workstream grounded: validate who owns each step and where a future scheduling solution would need to connect.

slides.title: 90 days: move from local dependency to repeatable execution

rows.right: Harbor Wiki gives consistent answers and playbooks
Echo and Spacesight reveal their routines
Spacesight surfaces store patterns during the week
Discovery output defines the integration path

slides.script: By 90 days, the change we are aiming for is structural. New hires should not experience six different onboarding journeys depending on who is rostered beside them. Store leaders should not need to guess what the best managers do differently. The COO should not be learning about last week’s shop floor after the opportunity has passed. Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki create a repeatable system for seeing, hearing, and teaching the standard. Scheduling remains an adjacent workstream, with a concrete integration path rather than a vague complaint.

slides.title: Alivia turns the evidence into an executable proposal

steps.label: Evidence
steps.text: Spacesight and Echo identify what is happening.

steps.label: Standard
steps.text: Harbor Wiki codifies what should happen.

steps.label: Plan
steps.text: Discovery defines stores, workflows, and gaps.

steps.label: Proposal
steps.text: Alivia packages the rollout into a client-ready proposal.

slides.script: Alivia matters because the COO does not only need insight; RetailCo needs a joined-up proposal that can be reviewed, funded, and executed. The flow is straightforward. Spacesight and Echo create the evidence base. Harbor Wiki turns that evidence into standard ways of working. The discovery work defines which stores, workflows, and open items are in scope, including scheduling. Alivia then packages the pieces into a coherent proposal, so we are not leaving RetailCo with disconnected product notes and asking operations to stitch the story together.

slides.title: What we must confirm before rollout

cards.heading: Store sample
cards.body: Which stores represent high, low, and typical execution?

cards.heading: Data boundaries
cards.body: What capture, privacy, and retention rules apply?

cards.heading: Operating cadence
cards.body: How will managers review and act on signals?

cards.heading: Scheduling scope
cards.body: Which roster steps are process versus system constraints?

slides.script: Before we ask RetailCo to commit to a broader rollout, we should answer four practical questions. First, which stores give us a fair comparison across strong, weak, and typical execution? Second, what are the boundaries for vision and conversation capture across APAC, including privacy and retention? Third, who will actually use the signals each week, and in what management cadence? Fourth, how much of the scheduling pain is caused by tooling, and how much by ownership, timing, and cross-team handoffs?

slides.title: Ask: approve a two-week discovery with operations
slides.subtitle: Goal: define the 30 / 60 / 90-day RetailCo standardisation proposal
bullets: Select representative stores and operations owners
Map Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki scope
Document scheduling workflow and open integration needs
Use Alivia to package the rollout proposal
slides.script: Our recommended next step is a focused two-week discovery with RetailCo’s operations team. We would use that time to choose representative stores, confirm the data and governance boundaries, map the management routines, and document the scheduling workflow without pretending we are selling a roster engine. The output would be a practical 30, 60, and 90-day proposal built through Alivia, showing exactly how Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki help RetailCo move from 120 local versions of execution to one consistent operating standard.

approach.angle: Argue standardisation: the stores are running as many different businesses as there are branches. Make consistency the prize and the products the means.
approach.device: Structure as 30 / 60 / 90 days - three horizons of what changes.
approach.opener: Open with the one sentence you want them to remember, then justify it.
approach.close: Close by asking for a two-week discovery with their ops team.
